youtube.title: You Can't Tickle Yourself. Here's Why #Shorts
youtube.description:
Theo can tickle anyone into tears. Except himself.

When you move, your brain predicts what the touch will feel like and turns the feeling down, so your own fingers barely register. Someone else's touch comes with no prediction, so it tickles. Brain scans point to the cerebellum as the predictor. In a 1999 experiment, people tickled their own palm through a robot: adding a delay of up to a fifth of a second (200 ms) made the touch feel more ticklish. Why bother? Muting your own touch makes everyone else's stand out.

Would you build one, or let your sister do it?

Sources:
- Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith (1998), Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation, Nature Neuroscience 1(7): https://link.springer.com/article/10.1038/2870
- Blakemore, Frith & Wolpert (1999), Spatio-temporal prediction modulates the perception of self-produced stimuli, Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience 11(5): https://columbia.demo.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/spatio-temporal-prediction-modulates-the-perception-of-self-produ-3
- Full text of the 1999 study: https://Gwern.net/doc/psychology/neuroscience/1999-blakemore.pdf

Theo, Nia, Dad and the living-room evening are fictional.
